record.original_question: Is every simple polygon with n vertices illuminable by at most ceil(3n/5)-1 vertex pi-floodlights, with at most one floodlight placed at any vertex, where a vertex pi-floodlight is a light source located at a polygon vertex that illuminates an angular wedge of width pi?

evidence.quote: The following old conjecture of mine was believed to be true up to December, 2001, when I found a counterexample:
Conjecture 5 Any simple polygon with n vertices can be illuminated with d 3n 5 e − 1 vertex π-floodlights.

artifact.self_contained_problem: Let P be a simple polygon in the plane with n vertices. A vertex π-floodlight is a light source placed at a vertex v of P that illuminates the points of P lying inside some closed angular wedge of aperture π with apex at v (the direction of the wedge may be chosen independently for each floodlight, subject to the wedge being contained in the half-plane bounded by some line through v). At most one floodlight may be placed at any vertex of P. The polygon P is said to be illuminated by a collection of such floodlights if every point of P lies in the illuminated region of at least one floodlight.\n\nDecide whether the following statement is true: for every simple polygon P with n vertices, P can be illuminated by at most ⌈3n/5⌉ − 1 vertex π-floodlights, subject to the rule of at most one floodlight per vertex.
artifact.status_search_result: According to the source of the conjecture, a counterexample to the statement was found in December 2001, so the conjecture is known to be false (resolved in the negative). The problem of finding the correct optimal bound for vertex π-floodlight illumination of simple polygons appears to remain a topic of subsequent investigation.
